issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
At 77, Walter had spent most of his adult life believing the world was basically understandable if a man stayed alert, worked hard, and treated people decently. He had been a delivery driver for years, and the routines of the job suited him: familiar routes, loading docks he knew by sight, brief greetings with clerks and receiving staff, the steady movement of boxes from truck to doorway. The assault happened on an ordinary workday, which was part of what had stayed with him. He had pulled up for a delivery expecting nothing more than another stop. Instead, in the space of a few minutes, he was confronted and attacked. What had begun as a routine part of his route turned abruptly into a situation in which another person came at him and he was no longer in control. The fact that it happened while he was doing something so normal, in a setting he had always regarded as predictable, left a mark on him that was still present when he came for treatment.

In the days afterward, Walter found himself trying to get through by doing the opposite of stopping. He kept working, took pains to stay occupied, and filled his time as densely as he could. If there was paperwork to sort, errands to run, shelves in the garage to straighten, he did them. At work he lingered over loading tasks and looked for extra things to handle around the truck because being still felt dangerous in a way he struggled to explain. When his mind started drifting back toward the assault, he pushed it away quickly. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about what happened in any sustained way, he would not be able to handle it. So he cut off thoughts midstream, turned on the television, went out to the driveway, reorganized tools, or found some reason to leave the room.

His wife noticed another change long before he said much about it. Walter started eating more than usual, especially in the evening after work, moving from dinner to snacks and then back into the kitchen again without really being hungry. He described it less as enjoyment than as something to do with himself, a way to settle the agitation in his body and blunt the edge of his distress. He did not present this to himself as a problem so much as a practical measure: if he could keep his hands busy and his mind on something immediate, maybe the rest would stay contained.

As the months passed, what unsettled him most was not only the memory of being assaulted but what it seemed to say about him and the world. Walter had become unsure of his own judgment in a way that felt humiliating. He questioned whether he had missed warning signs, whether he should have handled the moment differently, whether he could trust himself to do the right thing if anything like that ever happened again. Even small decisions on his route sometimes stirred this doubt. Pulling into a delivery site, he could feel a moment of hesitation and think, You don't know what you're walking into. A part of him that had once relied on his own practical sense no longer felt solid.

Alongside that self-doubt was a broader sense that the rules he had lived by no longer held. He said, in effect, that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. Before the assault, routine had meant safety to him; afterward, the ordinary quality of the day when he was attacked became part of what frightened him. A loading area, a doorway, an otherwise unremarkable stop on his route could suddenly feel altered because it reminded him that terrible things could happen in places he had once regarded as manageable. His occupation put him directly into the kinds of environments where that realization was hardest to ignore. Each workday meant entering unfamiliar or semi-familiar spaces again, and although he continued to do it, he did so by forcing himself forward and then trying not to think too much about what those places now meant to him.

At home, Walter gave his wife very little of the story. He was not trying to deceive her; he was protecting himself from what he imagined would happen if he opened the door to it. He was certain that dwelling on the assault would overwhelm him. When she asked how he was doing, he often answered in practical terms-tired, busy, hungry-keeping the conversation moving so neither of them stayed with the subject for long. The cost of this had been a growing distance between them. She could see he was not himself, and he could see that she knew it, but he felt unable to risk saying more.

By the time he sought help, Walter was exhausted by the effort of holding everything at bay. He was still working, still keeping busy, still eating too much to calm himself, still shutting down thoughts before they fully formed, but these strategies had come to organize his days. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the recognition that his life had narrowed around trying not to think. He wanted some way to live with what happened without feeling that a single memory could undo him. What frightened him most was that if he stopped controlling it, even briefly, he would find that he was not strong enough to bear what came up. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to feel like a reliable man in a recognizable world again.
